t.ensemble mixte de ua pou@-9.4,-140.1:
Ua Pou looks like nothing else in the Pacific. Basalt spires, narrow as organ pipes, rise above the island in a crown of grey rock, some of them over a thousand metres high, and clouds often catch on them and turn the whole skyline into a stage set. This is the Marquesas, one of the most remote island groups on earth, about fifteen hundred kilometres northeast of Tahiti, and the first sight of them from the sea is a good argument for taking the long way round.

The islands have a tough, proud culture. Marquesan carvers are famous for tiki figures and for tattoo, and the old stone platforms called me'ae, once used for ceremonies, are hidden in the forest valleys. Missionaries and traders arrived in the nineteenth century and brought disease that cut the population catastrophically, yet the language and the arts survived. Today there are Marquesan festivals with dance, drumming and carving competitions, and the locals still speak about family lines and valleys with a deep sense of belonging.

The main village, Hakahau, sits on the north coast, and from there narrow roads climb and dip along the coast to the other villages. The roads are mostly concrete or tarmac, steep and winding, with sudden drops and views of the spires. Rain squalls blow through quickly, and the best conditions are between May and October. Most of the traffic you meet is pickups, horses and the occasional goat.

Be realistic about logistics: there are no big towns, fuel is limited to the villages, and you should ask in Hakahau before you head out. Boats and small planes link the islands, and visitors usually rent a vehicle locally rather than bringing their own. Eat the fresh fish, breadfruit and coconut-cooked dishes at small family guesthouses, and carry cash, because cards are not universally accepted.
t.medan@3.6,98.7:
Medan is the biggest city on Sumatra, a hot, humid, entirely unpretentious place that has been a boom town since the late nineteenth century, when the surrounding highlands and plains were turned into plantations for tobacco, rubber and, later, palm oil. The money of those years is visible in the buildings. The Maimun Palace, built in 1888 for the Sultan of Deli, is a yellow-and-gold mixture of Malay, Mughal and Italian styles, and the nearby Great Mosque, with its black domes, is one of the most elaborate in the country. The mansion of Tjong A Fie, a Chinese merchant who became the richest man in the region, is a fascinating glimpse into the city's multi-ethnic past.

Medan is also a city of food. Batak, Malay, Chinese and Indian influences meet at its stalls, and the city is known for durian, for noodle dishes and for bika ambon, a spongy honeycombed cake. Traffic is intense, with a mix of cars, becaks, which are motorised rickshaws, and an endless sea of scooters, so it is best to leave early and keep your attention on every side.

For a rider, Medan is the gateway to Lake Toba, the largest volcanic lake in the world, formed by an eruption about seventy-odd thousand years ago that was one of the greatest in Earth's history. The road to it runs up through palm plantations and then climbs through the cool highlands past Berastagi, with its volcanoes Sibayak and Sinabung, to the lake shore at Parapat, a journey of several hours that is slow because of trucks and traffic. From Parapat, a ferry crosses to Samosir, an island in the lake with Batak villages, traditional houses with sweeping roofs and stone tombs. The air up there is fresh and cool.

Fuel is plentiful in Medan and along the main roads. Roads can be potholed and slick after the afternoon rain, so allow plenty of time and avoid riding after dark. The driest months run from June to September.
t.ensemble mixte de nuku hiva@-8.9,-140.1:
The Marquesas Islands lie some fourteen hundred kilometres north-east of Tahiti, and they are the most remote inhabited islands in French Polynesia. Nuku Hiva, the largest, is a jagged tropical mountain of valleys, ridges and sheer green walls that fall into the sea. Its people carved stone and wood with great skill, and the island still has ceremonial platforms, called paepae, and giant stone figures, tiki, hidden in the forest. The Marquesas are being proposed for recognition as a mixed cultural and natural site, which is where the name of this point comes from.

Taiohae, the main village, lies in a great collapsed volcanic crater that forms a bay, with a waterfront and a cathedral that holds carved wooden panels from several islands. Herman Melville deserted a whaling ship here in 1842, spent weeks in the neighbouring Taipivai valley, and used the experience for his first novel, Typee. Across the island, on the north coast, Hatiheu has a beautiful bay and a ceremonial platform called Kamuihei, and the roads that link the villages rise over passes with wild views.

This is a place where a motorbike is both ideal and unavailable. The island roads are short, steep and winding, some paved and some concrete strips, with sharp hairpins and surfaces that can wash out in heavy rain. Hire bikes are not a given, so look for a local pension that can arrange transport, or travel by four-wheel drive with a guide. The weather is warm all year, with a wetter period from December to April, and trade winds that keep the air from feeling heavy.

Taiohae has a small town centre with a few shops, a market, fuel from a small station, and several family pensions where you eat fish, breadfruit, goat in coconut milk and raw fish in coconut. The village of Taiohae itself is only just over a thousand people, so choose your supplies with care, and expect prices to be higher than in Tahiti because everything arrives by ship. Mosquitoes and the tiny no-no sand flies can be fierce near the beaches, so carry repellent. Respect sacred sites, ask before entering any ceremonial ground, and do not remove stones or carvings.
t.mae sai@20.4,99.9: Mae Sai lies about 2 km south of Tachilek, Thailand. On the rides it is a waypoint the route is laid through. It is on "Mae Salong and Golden Triangle Loop".
t.berastagi@3.2,98.5: Berastagi lies about 11 km north of Kabanjahe, Indonesia. On the rides it is a waypoint the route is laid through. It is on "Lake Toba and Samosir Loop".
t.parapat@2.7,98.9: You find Parapat some 8 km east of Tomok Bolon in Indonesia. The nearest city is Pematangsiantar, about 36 km away. On the rides it is a waypoint the route is laid through. It is on "Lake Toba and Samosir Loop".
